strong_form: Credentialing systems select and train for reliability (low outcome variance), and in fields where payoffs are power-law distributed this selection lowers the expected count of extreme right-tail contributions compared with admitting or cultivating higher-variance people and methods.
weak_form: Schools reward consistency and penalize idiosyncratic profiles, so some high-variance people get screened out of credentialed paths.
refuted_if: Among top-percentile contributors in power-law fields (e.g. most-cited scientists, founders of the largest firms), credentialed low-variance performers are over-represented compared with high-variance or non-credentialed peers once base rates are controlled, or programs designed to widen variance yield no more tail outcomes than standard selection.

prior_art.citation: Big Think, 'Our Cult of Achievement Is Crushing the Genius Out of People' (excellence as quality control vs high-variance genius)
Gamermann et al., 'Power law distribution in High School Education' (power-law tails appear in science grades, not humanities)
iqmindware Substack, 'The Cognitive Power Curve' (ability itself is normally distributed; power law applies to outcomes)
Zuckerman, Scientific Elite (many US Nobel laureates trained under laureates in elite credentialed settings)

strongest_criticism: Elite credentialed pipelines produce a large share of right-tail scientific outcomes (Zuckerman's laureate lineages), which suggests credentialing concentrates tail talent rather than suppressing it. High variance also means many more failures, and nobody has shown that the extra tail gains from loosening selection outweigh the extra losses. As stated the claim is a plausible decision-theory argument without a direct empirical test.
